Join us to think big, build something awesome, and embrace the chaos of space exploration.
summary:
Our project, Mapping the Red Planet, focuses on the topographic analysis of Mars’s Tharsis Volcanic Province to support future human exploration. We developed an elevation-based topographic map using NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) – Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) Global Digital Elevation Model (DEM), with a spatial resolution of 463 meters.

Using ArcGIS, we processed the elevation data, classified different elevation ranges into color-coded categories, generated contour lines, and identified major topographic features, including Olympus Mons, Ascraeus Mons, Pavonis Mons, and Arsia Mons.

Our map addresses the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge by providing essential terrain information for preliminary landing site selection, astronaut route planning, elevation analysis, and terrain identification. It helps distinguish steep and gentle slopes, as well as high and low elevation regions.

This project is important because understanding Martian terrain is a key step towards safer human exploration, better mission planning, and identifying potentially suitable areas for future astronauts.
details:
Project Details – Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map

Our project, Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map, focuses on the topographic analysis of the Tharsis Volcanic Province of Mars. It works by transforming raw elevation data into a visual map that makes Martian surface features easier to understand and analyze.

We used NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) – Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) Global Digital Elevation Model (DEM), which has a spatial resolution of 463 meters. Using ArcGIS, we imported the DEM, extracted our study area, applied color-coded elevation classification, generated contour lines, and designed our final topographic map.

The map highlights major features, including Olympus Mons, Ascraeus Mons, Pavonis Mons, and Arsia Mons. Closely spaced contour lines indicate steep terrain, while widely spaced contours represent gentler slopes.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

The project can support preliminary landing site selection, astronaut route planning, elevation analysis, and identification of mountains, volcanoes, and depressions. Its intended impact is to contribute to safer and more informed human exploration of Mars by making important terrain information accessible and easier to interpret.

Tools and Technology:

Our primary software was ArcGIS, and our main dataset was NASA’s MGS–MOLA Global DEM, sourced through NASA Planetary Data System and USGS Astrogeology resources. The project involved GIS-based spatial data processing and visualization.

Creativity and Innovation:

The creative aspect of our project lies in transforming scientific elevation measurements into an understandable visual guide for potential human explorers. Instead of presenting raw numerical data, we used elevation shading, contours, and topographic labels to communicate the structure of the Martian landscape.

Factors Considered:

Our team considered elevation differences, terrain variations, major volcanic features, contour spacing, spatial resolution, and the potential usefulness of the map for future exploration. We also considered the limitations of the dataset, as its 463-meter pixel size is suitable for preliminary terrain assessment but not for identifying individual rocks.
